Which SIM card is best for Koh Samui? | AIS is the safer choice if you'll spend time in the hills, on the south and west coasts or on boat trips: it won Opensignal's coverage awards in August 2026. True (merged with dtac) is just as good in Chaweng, Lamai and Bophut and was fastest for downloads.
How much is a tourist SIM in Thailand? | About 449–499 THB for 8 days, 699 THB for 15 days and 1,199 THB for 30 days with unlimited data on AIS or True, as listed in October 2026. AIS also sells a 1-day pack for 49 THB and a 60-day pack for 1,599 THB.
Can I buy a SIM at Samui airport? | Don't count on it, especially for a late arrival: counter hours at Samui Airport are limited and change. If you connect through Bangkok, the AIS and True counters at Suvarnabhumi are the easiest option; on Samui, use an operator or phone shop in Chaweng, Lamai or Nathon with your passport.
Do eSIMs work on Koh Samui? | Yes. Travel eSIMs run on the AIS or True networks and work across the island once your phone is unlocked and eSIM-compatible. AIS and True also sell their own tourist eSIMs. Most travel eSIMs are data only, without a Thai number.
Do I need my passport to buy a SIM? | Yes. Every Thai SIM must be registered in person with your passport, and foreigners can hold up to 3 SIMs per operator. Tourist SIMs last a maximum of 60 days unless you re-verify your identity.
Is there mobile signal on Ang Thong tours? | Partly. You'll have signal for much of the crossing, but coverage around the outer islands of the marine park is patchy. Download what you need beforehand and keep your phone in a waterproof pouch.
Is Wi-Fi good enough to work from Koh Samui? | Yes, if you choose your base well. Hotels, cafés and coworking spaces in Bophut, Chaweng and Lamai have fibre, but hillside villas vary. Ask for a speed test from the room and carry an unlimited SIM as a hotspot back-up.
